---
title: "Validation summary"
description: "One table with every published event type, flight list column and measurement of OPDI, its headline accuracy, the reference data it was checked against, and links to the details."
---

This page lists every item that OPDI publishes with the default settings of
release v2.0.0: each event type, each column of the flight list and each
measurement. For each item it gives the single number to remember from its
validation, and links to the methods page that describes the method and its
limits.

## How to read the table

- **Item** is the event type, column or measurement as it appears in the data.
  A part in braces stands for a family: `xing-{radius}nm` covers `xing-40nm`,
  `xing-100nm` and the other rings, and `entry-{element}` covers
  `entry-taxiway`, `entry-apron` and the other airport areas.
- **Kind** says whether the item is an event type, a flight list column or a
  measurement.
- **Headline accuracy** names the measure and gives its value. It is the
  number given under "Headline accuracy" on the item's methods page.
- **Reference** is the independent data the item was compared with.
- **n** is the number of cases the value is computed over: flights, movements,
  crossings or time windows, depending on the item.
- **Details** links to the "Validation method" and "Limitations" sections of
  the item's methods page.

**"Not validated"** means that the item has not been compared with any
independent data, so OPDI cannot say how accurate it is. It does not mean the
item is wrong. For most such items no suitable reference exists: no available
dataset records, for example, the top of climb or the entry into a taxiway.
Each methods page says what would be needed to validate its items. Some items,
such as the aircraft type, are copied from another database rather than
computed, and some, such as the version columns, describe the data itself.

**Accuracy figures of different items cannot be compared with each other.**
Each figure is measured against its own reference data, on its own days and
airports, with its own measure. Three examples:

- The take-off and landing times are compared with airport records that are
  mostly rounded to the minute, so their share within 60 s says little about
  differences of a few seconds. The ring crossings are compared with records
  given to the second.
- The time milestones were measured at the 20 airports with the best ADS-B
  reception, so their figures are better than what can be expected elsewhere.
- Some figures count how often OPDI agrees with the reference; others, such as
  the point merge figure, come from a visual check of a small sample; the FIR
  crossings are compared with an exact calculation from the same boundaries,
  which checks the computation but not the boundaries.

Read the methods page of an item before using its figure.
